name: Seated Calf Raise
tierNote: Safety tier C (content.md appendix B: not in the A or B lists); census.json difficulty tier 1.

claims.text: Lower the heels slowly below the platform to a deep stretch and pause there. The bottom pause differs: Motra pauses briefly (1 s in its 2-1-2, c19), BarBend three seconds; both place it at the bottom, after the lowering, not after the lift.

quotes.text: Pause briefly at the bottom to feel the calf stretch.

quotes.text: Slowly lower your heels towards the ground, going as far down as comfortably possible to get a good stretch in the calf muscles. This is your starting position.

quotes.text: Unrack the machine and slowly lower your heels as far as possible to the floor, pausing for three seconds.

claims.text: Push through the balls of the feet to raise the heels as high as possible, extending the ankles.

claims.text: One source's common-mistakes list for the machine seated calf raise names, in this order: using momentum or bouncing at the bottom, incomplete range of motion, letting the ankles roll inward or outward, poor posture with a rounded back, and excessive weight compromising form.

quotes.text: Using momentum or bouncing at bottom
Incomplete range of motion
Allowing ankles to roll inward or outward
Poor posture with rounded back
Excessive weight compromising form

claims.text: Use controlled movements, controlling the descent and not bouncing, to protect the Achilles tendon.

quotes.text: Use controlled movements to protect Achilles tendon
Control the descent
Avoid bouncing

claims.text: Range: lower the heels to the deepest stretch below the platform and raise them to full ankle extension, using as large a range as possible; but the stretch should stay comfortable: one source warns that overstretching can cause tendon issues in the lower leg, and another lowers only to a slight stretch.

quotes.text: Lower heels to maximum dorsiflexion below platform level, then raise to full ankle extension where calves are fully contracted.
Ensure full but comfortable stretch without overstretching
Use as large a range of motion as possible; half reps get half results!
Do not overstretch your calves as this can cause tendon issues in the lower leg.
Now, slowly lower your heels down until you feel a slight stretch in your calves.

claims.text: Keep the knees bent at 90 degrees and the back straight; avoid leaning back, which takes work away from the calves.

quotes.text: Keep knees bent at 90 degrees
Maintain straight back
Avoid leaning back, as doing so takes work away from your calves.

claims.text: Breathe in while lowering and out while raising the heels.

quotes.text: Inhale during the lowering phase and exhale forcefully as you raise your heels.

claims.text: The calves are the target; seated, the soleus (inner calf) does most of the work because the gastrocnemius, which crosses the knee, is shortened and slackened.

quotes.text: A machine-based isolation exercise targeting the soleus and gastrocnemius muscles to build calf strength and hypertrophy; performed seated with knees bent for focused lower leg work.
quotes.where: unheaded intro paragraph under the title (above the About tab)

quotes.text: Seated calf raises mostly train the inner calf muscle (solues), because the outer calf muscle (gastrocnemius) is in a shortened position.
The soleus is the agonist or prime mover during seated calf raises. In other words, it’s the muscle doing most of the work.
quotes.where: Seated Calf Raise: The Basics, Soleus

quotes.text: Because it crosses the back of your knee, the gastrocnemius is in a somewhat slackened position during seated calf raises.
quotes.where: Seated Calf Raise: The Basics, Gastrocnemius

claims.text: In 14 untrained adults training one leg seated (knee bent 90 degrees) and the other standing for 12 weeks, the gastrocnemius of the seated leg did not grow significantly, while the soleus grew about the same on both legs.

quotes.text: Fourteen untrained adults conducted calf-raise training with one leg in a standing/knee-extended position and the other leg in a seated/knee 90°-flexed position at 70% of one-repetition maximum.
Each leg performed 10 repetitions/set, 5 sets/session, 2 sessions/week for 12 weeks.
Muscle volume significantly increased in all three muscles and the whole triceps surae for both legs (p ≤ 0.031), except for the gastrocnemius muscles of the seated condition leg (p = 0.147-0.508).

The changes in muscle volume were significantly greater for the standing than seated condition leg in the lateral gastrocnemius (12.4% vs. 1.7%), medial gastrocnemius (9.2% vs. 0.6%), and whole triceps surae (5.6% vs. 2.1%) (p ≤ 0.011), but similar between legs in the soleus (2.1% vs. 2.9%, p = 0.410).

claims.text: Heavy weights put a lot of stress on the thighs under the pad, which some find uncomfortable; getting the pads in the right place helps, but seated calf raises can still hurt the legs.

quotes.text: Using heavy weights puts a lot of stress on your thighs. As such, some people may find the seated position uncomfortable or awkward, affecting their exercise enjoyment.
quotes.where: Seated Calf Raise – Cons, Uncomfortable for Some People

quotes.text: Getting the pads in the right place can help with this problem, but even then, and especially if you are lightly muscled or very lean, seated calf raises can hurt your legs.
quotes.where: Seated Calf Raise – Cons, Uncomfortable for Some People

claims.text: Pick a weight you can lift for 10-12 reps with good form, and start light to master the form.

quotes.text: Start by selecting a weight you can lift for 10-12 reps with good form.

quotes.text: Start with light weight to master form

claims.text: One source gives the tempo 2-1-2, and its Tempo tooltip gives the order: lowering, bottom pause, lifting, top pause, in seconds. Read in that order: 2 s down, a 1 s pause at the bottom, 2 s up; the same page squeezes for one second at the top (c9).

quotes.text: The speed for each phase of the movement, written as four numbers (e.g., 3-1-2-0): eccentric (lowering), bottom pause, concentric (lifting), top pause. Each number represents seconds.

plate.viewWhy: Census view is side; the 90-degree knee under the pad (c1, c2), the vertical shin (c4) and the heels dropping below and rising above the platform (c7, c8, c12) read from the side. The top fault, bouncing at the bottom (c10, c11), shows only as speed, so the plate draws incomplete range of motion (c10, c12), the heels stopping part way.
plate.equipment: Seated calf raise machine (census calfMachine, compose, with the kneePad roller pad): knee pad lever snug across the thighs just above the knees (c1, c2), foot platform under the balls of the feet with the heels free (c3), safety lever and handles by the pad (c5, c6).
plate.start: Bottom of the rep: seated upright, back straight (c5, c13); knees bent at 90 degrees with the shins vertical (c1, c4); pad across the thighs just above the knees (c2); balls of the feet on the platform, hip-width, toes forward, heels below the platform at a deep but comfortable stretch (c3, c7, c12); hands on the handles (c5).
plate.end: Top of the rep: heels as high as possible, ankles fully extended (c8, c12); knees, shins, thighs and trunk unchanged (c13); the pad lifted by the thighs (c1).

mistake.what: Heels moving only part way: no deep stretch at the bottom or no full rise at the top.
mistake.why: The top fault, bouncing or using momentum at the bottom (Motra's common-mistakes item 1; controlled movements protect the Achilles tendon, c10, c11), shows only as speed, so the plate draws the next fault by the same steps: incomplete range of motion, next on Motra's list (c10), against its full range from maximum dorsiflexion to full ankle extension (c12).
mistake.rankNote: No source measures how often each fault happens. LR-31 step 2: using momentum or bouncing at the bottom (c10, c11). Candidates: the load is not a candidate, so Motra's list item "Excessive weight compromising form" (c10) is set aside; the pad and seat setting (c2, c17) is a setup choice. Step 1: no frequency word for a fault of this exercise. Set aside: Fitness Volt's "The seated calf raise is often overshadowed by the standing variation" and "the seated calf raise machine is generally less popular" are about the exercise; "usually tucked away in the corner of the gym" and "Most seated calf machines require very few adjustments" are about the machines; "some people may find the seated position uncomfortable" uses 'some'; its standing lines ("arguably the most common and popular choice") are another exercise. BarBend's "most people have a stubborn muscle group" and "some people skip calf training" are about training. Fitness Volt's machine guide's "the calf muscles are one of the most stubborn muscles, it’s recommended to train them often" is about the muscle and training. Also set aside from Fitness Volt's article: "The most critical calf training decision that most people have to make is choosing between seated and standing calf raises." (exercise choice); "training them often involves heavy loads" (load); "Performing seated calf raises typically requires access to specific gym equipment" and "they’re often awkward or inconvenient compared to using a machine" (equipment and free-weight versions); "Easier to master; less likely to result in form errors." (names no fault); "the calves tend to work hardest when standing" ('tend', muscles); "overweight people often have large calves", "women, who often don’t want big calves", "For most people, this means 2-3 calf workouts per week", "some people believe the gastrocnemius responds best to lower reps" and "train them hard and often" (people, programming, training). Motra's "Popularity Score" tooltip ("How commonly this exercise is used") is about the exercise. Peloton's "“The most common mistake I see is people moving too quickly or bouncing through the motion,” Matt says." (read, not cited) is not counted for this card: Peloton's seated version is a chair with the feet flat on the floor and its main version is the standing bodyweight raise, so for the plate-loaded seated machine it is another version (R-LB7-5). Counted, it would name the same fault this card already ranks first (Motra's list item 1), so only the step number would change (1 instead of 2), not the pick or drawable. Step 2: one named fault is tied to harm: using momentum or bouncing at the bottom (Motra's list item 1, c10), by Motra's "Use controlled movements to protect Achilles tendon" (c11; D-SUP-PROTECT: the cue that corrects the fault protects a named body part); Motra's cues "Control the descent" and "Avoid bouncing" (c11) correct the same fault. Set aside at step 2: Fitness Volt's "Do not overstretch your calves as this can cause tendon issues in the lower leg." (c12): 'issues' is not an LR-31 harm word, and overstretching is on no common-mistakes list; read as harm, it would still lose step 2's first tie-break (the one on a common-mistakes list). Motra's "When to Avoid" item "Lower back pain if posture poor" is a condition, not a harm tie for its list item 4 ("Poor posture with rounded back"); read as one, the rounded back would lose to bouncing on the list order ("the earlier on a list that names both"). Fitness Volt's "Using heavy weights puts a lot of stress on your thighs" and "seated calf raises can hurt your legs" (c17) are about the load and the pads, not a fault of the set; its "seated calf raises are very back-friendly and suitable for exercisers with lower back pain" names no fault, and its standing lines ("Keep your knees slightly bent but stable throughout the exercise to avoid strain.", the spinal compression and "could even cause back pain") are another exercise; Motra's "Use safeties for heavy loads." is equipment, its "Avoid if acute Achilles or ankle injury present" a condition, and its tooltip "Conditions, injuries, or situations where this exercise should be avoided or modified." names no fault; BarBend's "help protect your Achilles tendon against possible injury" and "help prevent calf strains" are benefits of calf training, and "repetitive stress on your feet" is the jump rope, another exercise; Peloton's harm lines ("reduce injury risk", "reducing the risk of ankle sprains", the Achilles overuse study line, "especially when joint movement is painful") are benefits and its isometric variation; its "Avoid leaning back, as doing so takes work away from your calves." (c13) states no harm; Motra's other list items, "Incomplete range of motion" and "Allowing ankles to roll inward or outward" (c10), are tied to no harm (Fitness Volt's "half reps get half results!" states no harm). drawable false: bouncing and momentum show only as speed (LR-31). The plate draws the next fault by the same steps: step 2 has no other candidate tied to harm, so step 3's first remaining fault on Motra's list, the one common-mistakes list written for this exercise, decides: incomplete range of motion (c10, c12), which the side view shows as the heels stopping part way. (Reading held for the lead: if Fitness Volt's 'tendon issues' or Motra's 'Lower back pain if posture poor' were read as harm ties, step 2 would give the plate fault instead: overstretching, or the rounded back, list item 4. Both are set aside here on LR-31's literal harm words and the face_pull 'When to Avoid' precedent.) The ankles rolling in or out (list item 3) is sideways and needs a front view. handlingMistakes[0] stays bouncing; [1] incomplete range; [2] the ankles rolling, in Motra's list order.

tempo.text: Down 2 and up 2 are Motra's 2-1-2 (c19, WEAK), read in its Tempo tooltip's order: lowering, bottom pause, lifting, top pause (R-LB6-2, R-LB6-7). Its 1 s bottom pause matches its "Pause briefly at the bottom to feel the calf stretch." (c7) and sits at the stretch, so it is named here and not written in pause (LR-33); BarBend pauses three seconds at the bottom (c7). Pause 1 is the pause right after the lift, sourced: Motra's "Squeeze calves at the top for one second." (c9); Fitness Volt's "pause for a moment" there (c9) agrees.

grip.type: Hands on the handles, or on the sides of the seat, for stability (c5).
grip.note: Hand archetype balance: the hands steady the body and work the safety lever (c6); no hand zoom needed. No source gives a hand width, thumb or wrist position.

setup.step: Sit with the pad snug across your thighs, just above the knees.
Balls of your feet on the platform, hip-width, heels hanging off.
Grip the handles. Press through your toes and release the safety lever.
Put the safety back on after the set, before unloading.

posture.point: Lower slowly to a deep, comfortable stretch.
Push through the balls of your feet to raise your heels high.
Squeeze your calves at the top for one second.
Breathe in as you lower, out as you raise.

handlingMistakes.fix: Lower to a deep stretch, then raise your heels high.

rows.means: The inner calf muscle, the soleus, does most of the work.
Heavy weights put a lot of stress here.
rows.fix: Set the pad just above your knees.

risks.risk: Achilles: use controlled movements to protect it.
Overstretching your calves can cause tendon issues.
Heavy weights stress the thighs and can hurt your legs.

zooms.right: Pad snug across the thighs, just above the knees.
Heels from a deep stretch to as high as possible.

libraryDiff.why: calves primary matches every read source (c15); the soleus does most of the work seated (c15, c16). No secondary muscle is named by a read source.

loadProgression.text: Start light to master the form. Pick a weight you can lift 10-12 times with good form.

Anchor: Motra's machine seated calf raise page, read in full (How to Perform, Coaching Tips, Tempo with its tooltip, Range of Motion, Safety, Common Mistakes). Fitness Volt's seated-vs-standing article and its machine seated calf raise guide, BarBend's best-calf-exercises page (its seated calf raise section) and StrengthLog's seated calf raise page were read in full, and the Kinoshita 2023 abstract through efetch.

Shared card: get-in-out (shared/get-in-out.json @ 6d253b9e) lists seated_calf_raise in appliesTo; it is cited, not copied (LR-29). Its steps (set safety stops if the machine has them, pins fully in, sit and pick a weight you can control, ease the weight back to rest) and its note that on plate-loaded seated_calf_raise the stack-slam step reads as 'return the weight gently' cover getting in and out. This card's own setup lines on the safety lever (setup[3], setup[4]) rest on Motra's steps (c6), fetched for this card.

Stretch depth conflict (c12): Motra lowers to maximum dorsiflexion with a full but comfortable stretch and no overstretching; Fitness Volt's article says as far down as comfortably possible; Fitness Volt's machine guide lowers to a slight stretch and warns that overstretching can cause tendon issues. The card says a deep, comfortable stretch.
Bottom pause: Motra pauses briefly (1 s in its 2-1-2) and BarBend three seconds at the bottom (c7). Neither is the pause field (LR-33); both are named in plate.tempo.text.

The Achilles and thigh feel rows are place + the source's fault or stress + fix (LR-6). No read source for this exercise gives a stop line, so no row says stop (R-LB6-6). No shared red-flag box covers the ankle or thigh, so redFlags is empty.

Read and not cited: ACE's Calf Raise page (exercise-library/294) is a seated straight-leg selectorized machine, another exercise; Peloton's calf-raise article gives a chair version with the feet flat on the floor, another version. BarBend's seated-calf-raise URL 404s; Fitness Volt's seated-calf-raise URL serves an image.
